description: Space Mission Design Game- this is the one we hoping on
summary: Space missions are not designed one decision at a time. Every part added to a spacecraft changes its mass, power draw, cost and data return, and these limits push against each other. I noticed that most student tools teach only one piece of this, usually orbits. AETHEL // JPL puts the whole problem in front of the player. You pick a target (Low Earth Orbit, the Moon or Mars), choose a launch vehicle, and fit power, communications, instruments, propulsion and a chassis. Live gauges show how each choice changes the mission, and a launch check decides whether it goes. An on-board Advisor then explains why a design works or fails, for example why a nuclear power source is wasteful in Low Earth Orbit. The vehicle limits and components are based on NASA and JPL material. I built it as a solo participant for the Space Mission Design Game challenge.
details:
What it does. AETHEL is a browser-based simulator for learning mission trade-offs. The player starts with a goal and a budget, then builds a spacecraft piece by piece. Four gauges (mass, power, budget and data throughput) update after every choice, so the cost of each decision is visible straight away. When the design is ready, a launch sequencer runs a strict GO / NO-GO check against the launch vehicle’s limits.

How it works. The game keeps one shared state for the whole mission. Each component carries its own mass, power, cost and data values, and the gauges are recalculated from that list. Launch vehicles have payload limits and base costs. For missions beyond Earth orbit, the game uses C3 departure energy and Hohmann transfer ideas to decide how demanding a trip to the Moon or Mars is. The Advisor compares the player’s choices with the mission and gives a plain-language reason, not just a pass or fail. It also simulates battery drain during an orbital eclipse to teach depth-of-discharge limits.

Why it matters. I wanted students to feel the trade-off, not memorise it. A heavier instrument is a better instrument, until it no longer fits on the rocket. The Advisor is there to explain the reason behind each failure, because that is where most of the learning happens.

Tools. HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript, with no backend and no external libraries, so it runs from one link in any browser. The Web Audio API provides sound feedback. [Add one sentence on how you tested it, for example “I tested it on [N] missions and fixed [specific bug].”]

What was my own work. The idea, the choice of challenge, the mission rules, the component list and the teaching examples are mine. [Add what is true, such as: “I chose every component value and checked the vehicle limits against NASA sources.”]

Limitations. This is a simplified teaching model, not a flight simulator. Orbital mechanics are approximated, and the numbers are meant to show relative trade-offs, not to design a real spacecraft. Future versions could add more missions and more NASA-sourced parts.
